summary:
An EVA is most dangerous task an astronaut can perform.
During every Apollo moonwalk, flight controllers in Houston kept recalculating one thing: can the crew still walk back to safety? On Mars a radio signal takes up to 22 minutes each way, so that answer arrives too late. M.H.U.D. (Martian Head-Up Display) moves the calculation to the crew.
M.H.U.D. is a browser-based EVA planner and helmet display. It runs on real Mars terrain reconstructed from Curiosity images and cross-checked against the HiRISE elevation model. The crew plans a route over ground the suit can walk, checks it go / no-go against NASA EVA planning rules, then walks it in first person while the reserve on return is recalculated at every step. When the reserve runs out, the display says "Turn back now" on the spot.

Every value in the app is labelled as real data, model, simulation or assumption, with its source. A map shows where it is dangerous. M.H.U.D. shows whether you make it back.
details:
M.H.U.D. walks a crew through one EVA in five steps:

1. Mission: a science request from Earth at a real Curiosity site (Murray Buttes, Gale crater).

2. Plan: pick up to three sample spots on the map. The planner draws the fastest route that keeps every rule, shows where the ground is too steep and where radio contact is lost, and gives time, consumables and the reserve on return. The crew can place a radio relay; contact is recalculated at once (for spot 06, time without contact drops from 3 h 14 to 34min or less, depending on where the relay stands).

3. Go / no-go: seven checks on the planned route. Five are hard rules (slope, distance, way home, excursion length, solar storm time to shelter); two are cautions (radio shadow, and a slope check of the same route in an independent HiRISE elevation model).

4. Walk: first person through the helmet on the real terrain. The reserve on return is recalculated at every step. Off the route, the display plans the way from where the crew stands. A turn-back line on the small map shows the edge of the ground from which the crew still gets home with reserve. When the reserve reaches zero, the display says "Turn back now" and skips the remaining stops.

5. Debrief: planned against actual, broken rules, samples taken.

HOW IT WORKS

Terrain: the Access Mars 3D model of Murray Buttes (built from Curiosity Mastcam and Navcam images) is turned into a 0.5 m grid of height and slope. We aligned it to the HiRISE 1 m elevation model (about 2 m position error) so that every route can be checked against a second, independent dataset.

Route: Dijkstra over the grid. Ground steeper than 20° is closed (NASA EVA-EXP-0042), and stretches without radio contact cost more.

Radio: line of sight over the terrain from the suit antenna to the rover, or to a relay that sees the rover. The method was checked against measured radio loss on Apollo 15.

Effort and consumables: the Pandolf walking-effort equation (used by NASA JSC for EVA workload) scaled to Mars gravity, with body and load from a NASA Mars suit study. Oxygen, CO2 removal, cooling water and battery are drawn step by step. The way home counts at 1.2x effort (Apollo planning rule).
One set of numbers feeds Plan, Go / no-go, Walk and Debrief. Nothing is precomputed: change the stops, the relay or the pace, and everything is recalculated.

BENEFITS

- Safety: the walk-back decision no longer waits for Earth. The crew sees on the spot whether it can still get home, and the turn-back call comes before supplies run out.

- Quality of planning: rules are checked before the EVA starts, and planned against actual afterwards shows where the plan was too optimistic.

- Honesty: every value carries a label (real, model, simulated, assumption) and a source on the Sources page. Rule values come from Moon and Apollo planning, because NASA has not set them for Mars yet, and the app marks them.

WHAT WE HOPE TO ACHIEVE

The structure stays the same as better data arrives: a HiRISE terrain for any site, live weather and solar storm alerts, live suit telemetry, Mars-specific EVA limits, and positioning without GPS (rover and relay as radio beacons).

LIMITS WE STATE and DEMO TRADE-OFFS

Suit time runs 76x faster in the demo so that a 128 m site gives hours of EVA. The position in the walk is known exactly. Heart rate and suit pressure are simulated. The radio relay

device is simulated; its effect is calculated as line of sight.

TOOLS

JavaScript, Three.js and Vite (web app, GitHub Pages); Python with numpy, Pillow and DracoPy (terrain preprocessing, HiRISE alignment); Vitest and Playwright (tests and recording);
dataRefs: Access Mars 3D terrain of Murray Buttes (NASA/JPL-Caltech with Google Creative Lab, built from Curiosity Mastcam/Navcam images)
HiRISE DTM DTEEC_040770_1755_039280_1755_U01 (NASA/JPL/University of Arizona, PDS)
Curiosity RAD dose rate, 0.67 mSv per day (Hassler et al. 2014)
Curiosity REMS air temperature, sol 1440 (PDS Atmospheres, MSL-M-REMS-5-MODRDR-V1.0)
Curiosity photos (NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS) on the mission requests
EVA-EXP-0042 Rev B, Exploration EVA System Concept of Operations (slope 20°, 6 h / 8 h EVA, pace)
OCHMO-TB-020 Rev E, Radiation Protection Technical Brief (back in shelter within 2 h in a solar storm)
Bellcomm B70 10028, Apollo 15 EVA Capability and Constraints Envelopes (work rates, way home at 1.2x)
Ogilvie et al., Mars Spacesuit Mass Requirements, ICES-2026-127 (body, load, suit mass)
Oliver et al., Mars Exploration PLSS Schematic Study, ICES 2026 (backpack capacity)
Kim et al., NASA JSC, IEEE EMBC 2024 (Pandolf equation for EVA workload)
Apollo 15 Mission Report, Suppl. 6, MSC-05161 (radio shadow from terrain, measured vs predicted)
NASA Mars Fact Sheet (gravity 3.71 m/s², sol length)
projectRefs: ESA Gaia DR2 (ESA/Gaia/DPAC), with Hipparcos-2 and Tycho-2
Access Mars app and assets (Google Creative Lab, Apache-2.0)
Pandolf equation terrain coefficient (secondary source, marked as assumption in the app)
